questions.q: Why does `assert counts == {'00': 500, '11': 500}` fail most of the time even on a correct Bell-state circuit?
options: Measurement outcomes are probabilistic, so raw shot counts vary run to run even when the circuit is correct
Qiskit forbids comparing dictionaries with assert
The Bell state never produces the 00 or 11 outcome
Simulators always return exactly 512/512 splits
questions.explain: Measurement is inherently probabilistic, so repeated runs of even a perfectly correct circuit produce different raw counts. An exact-match assertion on counts will fail almost every time; the fix is a statistical test with a justified tolerance, covered in Chapter 2.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three properties the lesson identifies as making quantum code genuinely different from typical classical code?
options: Measurement outcomes are inherently probabilistic
Real hardware noise profiles exist and drift over time
The quantum SDK ecosystem changes with unusually frequent breaking changes
Quantum code cannot be stored in a version control system like Git
questions.explain: Quantum code is ordinary text and can absolutely be version-controlled with Git (Chapter 4 covers this in depth). The three real differentiators are probabilistic measurement, hardware noise, and SDK instability.

questions.q: A circuit passes cleanly on a noiseless simulator but shows visibly skewed counts when run on real IBM hardware. What does the lesson say this most likely reflects?
options: The simulator must be broken
Real hardware noise (gate error, decoherence, readout error), which differs from and can drift relative to an ideal simulator
The circuit definitely has a logic bug
Shots were set too high
questions.explain: Noise on real hardware -- gate error, decoherence, readout error -- can skew measured counts away from the ideal simulator result even when the circuit logic is correct. Distinguishing a noise effect from a genuine logic bug is exactly the debugging skill built in Chapter 2.

questions.q: Which specific historical example does the lesson cite as evidence the quantum SDK ecosystem is unusually unstable?
options: Python itself changing from version 2 to 3
Qiskit's 0.x to 1.0 transition, which removed and renamed core APIs
NumPy deprecating complex number support
Jupyter notebooks being retired in favor of plain scripts
questions.explain: The lesson cites Qiskit's 0.x to 1.0 transition as a concrete example of a breaking change that removed and renamed core APIs -- exactly the kind of churn that pinned dependencies (Chapter 4) protect against.

questions.q: According to the lesson's mapping table, what is the quantum-specific adaptation of classical dependency pinning?
options: Pin only the Python interpreter version and nothing else
Avoid pinning altogether since quantum SDKs update too often to track
Pin the SDK version and also record the backend/simulator version, since numerical behavior can depend on both
Pin the operating system version only
questions.explain: The lesson's table specifically notes that quantum dependency management must pin both the SDK version and the backend/simulator version, because numerical results can depend on either one changing -- a more demanding requirement than typical classical pinning.
